newsitem.title: INDIA: Tussle in Dunlop India hides other woes.
newsitem.headline: Tussle in Dunlop India hides other woes.

text.p: A divisive management battle at Dunlop India Ltd masks problems with the tyre-maker's declining market share and growing competition, analysts said on Thursday.

"Dunlop's market share in the overall tyre segment fell to 1.4 percent in FY96 (financial year ending March 31, 1996) from 15 percent in 1989/90," Sandeep Dhingra, tyre analyst at SSKI Securities told Reuters.
"There's a fundamental problem with the company -- it's cash strapped and unable to add fresh capacities," said Rajesh Samtani, tyre analyst at Nucleus Securities.
"In truck and bus tyres, which make up almost 70 percent of the tyre market, Dunlop has been losing its market share," said Hitesh Merchant, analyst at N.H.Securities.
In this segment, Dunlop's share has fallen to 5.4 percent in 1995/96 from 11.7 percent in 1989/90, he said.
The firm's managing director Murli Shukla and its chief financial officer Anju Madeka quit the company this week after a public stand-off with chairman Manohar Chhabria.
Chhabria told Reuters in Dubai, where he is based, that no personal disagreement had caused the Shukla resignation.
Shukla, contacted by telephone at his home in Calcutta, refused to answer any questions.
Chhabria owns 44 percent of Dunlop India, Indian financial institutions have 33 percent and the balance equity is held by retail investors.
Chhabria forecast the company would make net profits of between 450 million and 500 million rupees in fiscal 1996/97, up from 390 million in the 15 months to March 31, 1996.
"That's a tough target," said SSKI's Dhingra. "Nobody has those margins."
"I doubt they'll achieve that," said V.S. Fernando, chief executive officer at Seahorse Trinity Aarthik Research. "They have a credibility problem."
The research firm said Dunlop had a price-earnings (P/E) ratio of 1.5 based on first-half earnings ending September 30, 1996 against the tyre industry P/E average of 20.
On Thursday afternoon Dunlop shares were trading at 30 rupees on the Bombay Stock Exchange, down about 34 percent since the beginning of 1996.

"The tyre industry is expected to see a growth of at least 20 percent by value in the current financial year but because of huge competition, margins are likely to come under pressure," said an analyst at securities firm James Capel B&K.
He said Dunlop faced competition from local tyremakers like Apollo Tyres, MRF Ltd and CEAT Ltd, who were raising production capacities.
"Then there are global players like Goodyear and Michelin, which are focusing on truck radials. Pirelli and Bridgestone are also trying to get a hold on the Indian market," he said.
Analysts attributed Dunlop's problems to poor management.
"At least partly because of the instability at the top, Dunlop has become a poorly managed company and has been steadily losing market share," the Business Standard said.

"Although its profits last year were modest, even these were suspect with Dunlop really fighting with the Tyre Corporation of India for the last place in the tyre companies' league table," it said in an editorial on Thursday.
An official from Dunlop's headquarters in Calcutta said the tyre business brought in only 62 percent of revenue. Industrial products like steel belting and hoses accounted for the balance 38 percent.
The company's Monday statement said an audit of management and financial performance had been ordered after Shukla's exit.
